blocks.content: Quiz: What does the -u flag do in git push -u origin main?
Tap an option below to answer:
Forces the push even if the remote has commits your local branch does not have
Forcing a push requires --force, which is a different and more dangerous flag. The -u flag has nothing to do with overriding remote history.
Forcing a push requires --force, which is a different and more dangerous flag. The -u flag has nothing to do with overriding remote history.
Sets the upstream tracking so future git push and git pull commands work without specifying the remote and branch
Correct. After git push -u origin main, Git remembers that this branch tracks origin/main. Future pushes and pulls on this branch just need git push or git pull — no extra arguments.
Correct. After git push -u origin main, Git remembers that this branch tracks origin/main. Future pushes and pulls on this branch just need git push or git pull — no extra arguments.
Uploads only files that changed since the last push, skipping unchanged files
Git always sends the commits the remote does not have — the -u flag does not change what gets uploaded. It changes how future push and pull commands behave.
Git always sends the commits the remote does not have — the -u flag does not change what gets uploaded. It changes how future push and pull commands behave.
Creates a new branch on GitHub called origin
origin is the name of the remote connection, not a branch. The -u flag sets up tracking between your local branch and the remote branch — it does not create anything new.
origin is the name of the remote connection, not a branch. The -u flag sets up tracking between your local branch and the remote branch — it does not create anything new.
